tasks.short: Plan meeting dates, read committee papers, take part in meetings, write the minutes as secretary, check them, and send them to members.

steps.what: Mathematics lecturer plans committee meeting dates by e-mail
Mathematics lecturer reads committee papers on policies and academic issues
Mathematics lecturer asks members' consent to record the meeting and starts the recording
Mathematics lecturer serves on academic or administrative committees in meetings
Mathematics lecturer writes the minutes as committee secretary

loop.input: The meeting transcript, recorded with members' consent, and the agenda.
loop.output: Draft minutes with decisions and actions per agenda item.
loop.check: Code flags any decision or action whose words are not found in the transcript. The lecturer checks each decision and action against the transcript and the meeting, its wording, owner and date, and edits every item.
loop.stop: One draft per meeting; if rejected, the lecturer writes the minutes.
loop.why_not_simpler: A template gives headings, not what was decided.

steps.what: Mathematics lecturer checks the final minutes
Mathematics lecturer places the checked minutes in the committee's shared folder, which notifies members; e-mailed today

tasks.design: Meeting dates are set with a calendar poll ({CALENDAR}). When the lecturer is secretary, a bounded step drafts minutes from the transcript recorded with members' consent; decisions and actions not found in the transcript are flagged, and the lecturer edits every item. Once checked, the minutes go to the committee's shared folder, which notifies members. Reading papers and taking part in meetings stay with the lecturer.
tasks.previous_blocker: Dates were set by e-mail and minutes written from handwritten notes.
tasks.enabler_now: Speech recognition and language models draft minutes that can be checked against the transcript.
tasks.still_hard: Members may not consent to recording.
tasks.human_edge: Moving a committee towards a decision.

evidence.claim: Language models can draft minutes from a transcript, and code can flag items not found in it.
Recording meetings processes members' personal data and needs a lawful basis such as consent.

assumptions: Boundary: from the committee term to minutes sent; carrying out decisions is outside.
Input contract: members consent to recording; fallback is handwritten notes.
The lecturer is secretary for some committees.
Meetings do not get shorter. Members of most committees consent to recording; where they do not, minutes are written from notes. s6 keeps 20 for placing the minutes.
research_questions: How much of each drafted minutes is kept?

incremental.description: No new work: asking consent is shown as step s2b.

approvals.approved_version: The minutes exactly as checked by the lecturer in s5, placed once in the committee's shared folder for its members; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: members of the lecturer's committees do not consent to recording, so minutes are written from notes and s4 keeps 90 (9.0); high: a committee secretary with recorded monthly meetings (16.5).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Search the literature, read and study it, do the research, write the paper, format references to the journal style, check the manuscript, and submit it.

steps.what: Mathematics lecturer searches literature for the research question
Mathematics lecturer reads and studies the literature
Mathematics lecturer conducts research in the field
Mathematics lecturer writes the paper to publish findings

loop.input: The lecturer's own text of the paper, section by section.
loop.output: Suggested language edits for clarity and grammar.
loop.check: Code compares formulas and theorem statements before and after and drops any suggestion that changes them; the lecturer accepts or rejects each edit.
loop.why_not_simpler: Spelling checkers do not fix unclear sentences.

steps.what: Mathematics lecturer formats references and the manuscript to the journal style
Mathematics lecturer checks the final manuscript
Mathematics lecturer submits the manuscript in the journal portal

tasks.design: A literature search tool with topic summaries and saved alerts ({OTHER}) suggests papers; every reference must resolve by DOI or catalogue record before it is kept. A bounded step suggests language edits on the lecturer's own text; any change to a formula or theorem is dropped and the lecturer accepts each edit. A reference manager with the journal's style file formats references and the manuscript. Research, proofs and the decision to submit stay with the lecturer.
tasks.previous_blocker: References were formatted by hand and searches repeated site by site.
tasks.enabler_now: Research search tools summarise topics; reference managers apply journal styles.
tasks.still_hard: Suggested references can be invented and must be resolved.

evidence.claim: Scopus AI gives topic summaries and foundational papers.
Invented references pass plagiarism checks unflagged.

assumptions: Boundary: from the research question to the manuscript submitted; peer review is outside.
Input contract: university licence for the search tool; fallback is manual search.
Every reference resolves by DOI or catalogue record.
research_questions: Do formatting rounds with journals fall?

already_counted.description: Mathematics lecturer reviews suggested language edits.

incremental.description: Mathematics lecturer resolves suggested references by DOI.

approvals.approved_version: The manuscript exactly as checked by the lecturer in s6, submitted once in the portal of the named journal; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: a short paper in a familiar field with few references, so s1 keeps 80 and s5 keeps 60 (9.5); high: a long survey paper with many references (15.5).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Collect lecturers' availability and course needs, build the schedule, resolve clashes, check it, and enter it in the central timetable.

steps.what: Lecturers enter availability and course needs in the timetabling system's form
Mathematics lecturer collects lecturers' availability and course requirements from the timetabling form and chases missing ones; by e-mail today
Mathematics lecturer develops department and course schedules in a spreadsheet
Mathematics lecturer resolves clashes and decides trade-offs
Mathematics lecturer checks the final schedule
Mathematics lecturer publishes the checked schedule in the central timetable from the timetabling system; typed in today

tasks.design: Lecturers enter availability and course needs in a form in the university timetabling system ({OTHER}), so they are not collected by e-mail. Fixed rules on room size, lecturer availability and no clashes between courses in the same year build a first schedule and list clashes. The lecturer resolves clashes; once checked, the schedule is published in the central timetable from the same system instead of being typed in again.
tasks.previous_blocker: Needs came by e-mail and the schedule was built in a spreadsheet and typed into the central system.
tasks.enabler_now: Timetabling systems build schedules from rules and take availability forms.
tasks.still_hard: Shared lecturers across departments have conflicting needs.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing which colleague will swap a slot.
tasks.altitude: The lecturer resolves clashes instead of building the grid.

evidence.claim: Timetabling systems can build schedules from rules on rooms, availability and clashes.

assumptions: Boundary: from the term ahead to the schedule published; room building is outside.
Input contract: lecturers fill the form; fallback is e-mail.
Lecturers fill the form (s0) in about the time an e-mail took; their time is outside the lecturer's savings. s5 keeps 10 for the publication.
The lecturer checks the schedule before publishing.
research_questions: Do timetable changes after publication fall?

incremental.description: Mathematics lecturer keeps the scheduling rules current.

approvals.approved_version: The department and course schedule exactly as checked by the lecturer in s4, published once in the central timetable for that term; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: a small department where many lecturers still e-mail and rules fit few courses, so s1 and s2 keep 70 (33.5); high: a large department with many shared lecturers (52.3).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Meet staff on department matters, decide staffing and budget, approve requests, write reports for the faculty, and answer administrative e-mails.

steps.what: Mathematics lecturer performs department head duties in meetings with staff
Mathematics lecturer decides on staffing, budget and teaching assignments
Mathematics lecturer opens leave, expense and purchase requests from the approval list with budget and leave balance; e-mails with attachments today
Mathematics lecturer checks each request: days or amount, leave balance or budget, and purpose
Mathematics lecturer approves the checked requests; the workflow passes them to HR and finance
Mathematics lecturer writes reports and memos for the faculty
Mathematics lecturer answers administrative e-mails

tasks.design: Leave, expense and purchase requests reach the head through approval workflows in the HR and finance systems ({WORKFLOW}) with the budget and leave balance shown, so they are approved from one list instead of e-mails with attachments. Staff numbers, teaching load and budget figures for faculty reports come from the faculty dashboard ({BI}) instead of being collected by hand. Meetings, decisions and answering e-mails stay with the lecturer.
tasks.previous_blocker: Requests came by e-mail and report figures were collected by hand.
tasks.enabler_now: HR and finance systems route requests; faculty dashboards hold the figures.
tasks.still_hard: Unusual requests still come by e-mail.
tasks.human_edge: Settling a conflict between two colleagues.

evidence.claim: HR and finance systems can route requests for approval with balances shown.
Staff data in approval workflows are personal data and need a lawful basis.

assumptions: Boundary: from the department matter to e-mails answered; faculty decisions are outside.
Input contract: workflows set up by HR and finance; fallback is e-mail.
Decisions and the check of each request stay with the head. s3 keeps 40 because the requests are still opened and read; the list removes searching e-mails and attachments.
Staff submit requests in about the time an e-mail took.

incremental.description: Mathematics lecturer handles requests that fall outside the workflows.

approvals.approved_version: Each leave, expense or purchase request exactly as checked by the head in s3b, approved once in the workflow and passed to HR or finance; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: a small department where many requests still come by e-mail and dashboards miss figures, so s3 keeps 80 and s4 keeps 90 (2.6); high: a large department with many requests (8.8).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The mathematics lecturer keeps doing research, taking part in committees, resolving schedule clashes and leading the department; minutes from notes, hand-formatted references, spreadsheet grids and e-mailed requests shrink.
role.ambitious_version: A lecturer with more time for research.
